strengths: RAD is a simple and practically appealing training-free method: global reference retrieval, spatially constrained patch matching, and multi-layer frozen features form a coherent design that can incorporate new normal examples without retraining.

The empirical results are extensive and promising. RAD reports strong localization across MVTec-AD, VisA, and Real-IAD, particularly large Pixel-AP gains, and includes few-shot, data-scaling, backbone, resolution, component-ablation, per-category, and qualitative analyses.

The few-shot results suggest meaningful sample efficiency: with one MVTec-AD reference per category, RAD reaches 96.7 Pixel AUROC and 91.9 AUPRO while using a substantially smaller backbone than some specialized baselines.
The component ablation supports the main engineering choices: multi-layer features provide the largest gain, while global retrieval and spatial conditioning add complementary improvements.
The manuscript is generally clear and well organized, with a helpful pipeline figure, detailed benchmark tables, proofs in the appendix, and an honest acknowledgement of memory and retrieval costs.
weaknesses: The central theoretical conclusion is not established. Lemma 2.2 only shows that a decoder Jacobian must have large norm when it inverts a contractive bottleneck; it does not imply that the composed reconstruction map or its residual score is unstable. Indeed, Assumption 2.1 directly requires the residual map to vary by at most eta along benign directions, so decoder amplification may simply compensate for bottleneck contraction.

The claimed upper bound over reconstruction scoring is overstated. Proposition D.1 proves only that retrieval scores stored training embeddings as zero, while Proposition D.2 makes retrieval pointwise maximal among scores that are already 1-Lipschitz and zero on the memory. Reconstruction residuals are not shown to satisfy either condition, so these propositions provide no pointwise comparison on test anomalies and do not show that retrieval upper-bounds encoder-decoder pipelines.

The theory analyzes Euclidean distance to one fixed set, whereas actual RAD uses cosine dissimilarity, query-dependent global top-K selection, spatially varying candidate sets, and multi-layer fusion. Top-K set changes can be discontinuous, and cosine dissimilarity of normalized vectors is proportional to squared Euclidean distance rather than the analyzed distance. Consequently, the stated non-expansiveness guarantee does not directly apply to the proposed algorithm.

The empirical comparison is materially confounded by backbone strength. RAD uses the recent DINOv3 ViT-B/16, while competing methods generally use different and often older representations. The paper's own backbone study shows large performance variation, but it does not retrain or re-evaluate the strongest reconstruction baseline with the same DINOv3 encoder, nor compare against a plain DINOv3 nearest-neighbor baseline. Thus the experiments do not isolate the contribution of RAD's scoring design.

Reported results contain concerning inconsistencies between the main text and appendix. For example, RAD's MVTec mean changes from 99.6/99.8/99.0 and 94.9 AUPRO in Table 1 to 99.5/100.0/98.9 and 95.8 in Tables A5-A6; several UniAD VisA aggregates also differ substantially. The manuscript does not explain differing runs or protocols.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the layer-fusion weights are unspecified; there is no validation protocol explaining how highly dataset-specific K and neighborhood radii were selected; few-shot experiments use only one random seed without uncertainty over reference sampling; and the displayed code link is empty. Runtime and memory consumption are acknowledged as limitations but never quantified, despite storing several feature layers and retrieving up to 900 images.

The significance claims are broader than the evidence. Evaluation is largely on aligned industrial imagery, where location conditioning is especially advantageous; robustness to misalignment, semantic/logical anomalies, contamination of the normal memory, or genuine deployment distribution shifts is not tested. The 3D experiment uses only RGB and reports only F1 scores, so it offers limited support for generalization beyond 2D MUAD.

The impact statement is too cursory for an industrial anomaly detector. It does not discuss risks from false negatives, sensitivity to domain shift or contaminated references, or the need for human oversight in safety- or quality-critical deployment.

strengths: Soundness/empirics: RAD reports strong results across MVTec-AD, VisA, Real-IAD, and an RGB-only 3D-ADAM evaluation, covering standard, few-shot, and cold-start settings with multiple localization metrics and per-category results.
Practical significance: Eliminating task-specific optimization while allowing new normal examples to be added directly to memory is attractive for rapidly changing industrial deployments.

Presentation: The global-retrieval, spatial-conditioning, and multi-layer matching pipeline is understandable, and the appendix supplies pseudomathematical definitions, implementation settings, per-class tables, qualitative examples, and component ablations.

Empirical analysis: The data-scaling experiments are useful and show especially large localization gains in low-data regimes. The encoder and resolution study also makes RAD's dependence on foundation representations explicit.
Limitations: The authors honestly acknowledge memory and retrieval-latency costs and show qualitative failure modes under viewpoint and illumination changes.
weaknesses: Soundness—the central fidelity–stability conclusion does not follow from the analysis. Lemma 2.2 only says that a decoder must have large gain to invert a contractive bottleneck while the composite reconstruction map remains near-identity. Large gain in the decoder alone does not imply instability of the composite residual score. Indeed, Assumption 2.1 directly constrains R(z)-z to vary slowly along the designated benign directions, which points toward residual stability rather than the claimed unavoidable instability.

Soundness—the advertised upper bound over reconstruction methods is not proved. Proposition D.1 establishes only the trivial fact that nearest-neighbor distance is zero when a stored feature retrieves itself, whereas a reconstruction can have nonzero training residual. Proposition D.2 applies only to 1-Lipschitz scores that vanish on the memory; reconstruction residuals are not shown to satisfy either condition. Neither result yields an ordering of anomaly-detection performance.

Soundness—the theory analyzes distance to one fixed set under one norm, but the implemented RAD score uses cosine dissimilarity, multiple layers, spatially restricted candidate sets, and a top-K global reference set that changes with the query. The stated 1-Lipschitz guarantee therefore does not directly characterize the proposed algorithm.

Evaluation fairness: RAD uses a recent DINOv3 backbone and 448-by-448 inputs, while the principal table compares against heterogeneous published systems with different encoders and resolutions. The paper does not provide controlled same-backbone, same-resolution comparisons against strong retrieval and reconstruction baselines, so the gains cannot be attributed reliably to the proposed retrieval design.

Originality: Feature-memory nearest-neighbor anomaly detection, spatially aware matching, and multi-layer frozen features are all established ideas in PatchCore, SPADE, PNI, UniVAD, and related work. Global image retrieval followed by local matching is a reasonable combination, but the conceptual advance is incremental once the unsupported theoretical framing is removed.

Reproducibility: Dataset-specific K values ranging from 48 to 900 and different spatial radii are reported without a validation or selection protocol. Only one random seed is used, which is particularly inadequate for few-shot subsampling, and no uncertainty estimates or repeated trials are given.

Reproducibility and practicality: Although memory and latency are acknowledged, the manuscript gives no actual memory footprint, preprocessing cost, inference latency, or scaling curve. These measurements are important for a method storing all multi-layer patch embeddings and retrieving up to 900 images.

Ablations are limited to MVTec-AD and omit sensitivity to K, spatial radius, layer weights, memory size/compression, pooling percentage, and normalization. They also do not separate the benefit of DINOv3 and increased resolution from the method itself.

Presentation and claims: Statements that the results “overturn” the need for training and that retrieval “upper-bounds encoder–decoder pipelines” substantially exceed the evidence. RAD still relies on large-scale pretrained representations, and the experiments establish only that task-specific training was unnecessary for these selected benchmarks and settings.

Ethics: There is no major intrinsic ethical concern, but the impact statement dismisses all potential consequences despite an industrial detection setting where false negatives, distribution shift, and deployment overconfidence may affect safety or quality control. A brief discussion of such risks would be appropriate.

strengths: Soundness/empirics: RAD is simple and practically appealing, combining a frozen DINOv3 encoder with global image retrieval, spatially constrained patch matching, and multi-layer scores. Ablations show complementary improvements from multi-layer memory, global retrieval, and spatial conditioning.

Significance: Results are extensive across MVTec-AD, VisA, Real-IAD, 3D-ADAM, few-shot, and cold-start scaling settings. The strongest evidence is in localization: for example, RAD improves MVTec-AD pixel AP from Dinomaly's 69.3 to 75.6 and Real-IAD pixel AP from 42.8 to 53.7.

The few-shot results are compelling: with one reference per class, RAD reports 96.7 pixel AUROC and 91.9 AUPRO on MVTec-AD, exceeding the reported specialized few-shot baselines while using a relatively modest 86M-parameter backbone.

Presentation: The method is clearly motivated and described, with a useful system diagram, per-category results, qualitative maps, implementation settings, and an honest discussion of memory, latency, and RGB-only failure modes on 3D-ADAM.
Reproducibility is partly supported by reporting the encoder, extracted layers, image resolution, dataset-specific retrieval parameters, image-level pooling, software versions, hardware, and seed.

No major ethical concern is apparent. Reducing task-specific training could lower deployment cost, although the impact statement could discuss false positives and false negatives in safety-critical inspection more concretely.
weaknesses: Soundness/theory: The claimed fidelity-stability dilemma is not established by Lemma 2.2. A large decoder Jacobian does not imply that the residual score is unstable: the residual map has Jacobian I-J_R. Indeed, Assumption 2.1 explicitly makes R locally near-identity and therefore bounds changes in the residual map by eta along benign directions—the opposite of the subsequent instability narrative.

The advertised theorem that retrieval scores upper-bound reconstruction-residual scores is unsupported. Proposition D.1 instead gives S_ret <= S_rec only on stored normal features. Proposition D.2 makes S_ret pointwise maximal only among 1-Lipschitz scores that vanish on the memory, but reconstruction residuals need satisfy neither condition. None of these results provides a performance or anomaly-separation upper bound over reconstruction pipelines.

Originality is limited relative to established nearest-neighbor memory methods such as SPADE, PatchCore, and position-aware retrieval methods. Global prefiltering, local spatial neighborhoods, and multi-layer feature fusion form a useful combination, but the paper's claim of overturning the need for training is stronger than the methodological novelty supports.

The standard-setting comparison is incomplete for the central training-free claim: Table 1 omits strong training-free or classical retrieval baselines such as PatchCore and UniVAD, while these appear only in restricted few-shot or 3D comparisons. A same-backbone, same-resolution comparison against PatchCore-style retrieval and against a trained reconstruction head on DINOv3 is essential to separate RAD's design gains from DINOv3 and 448x448 inputs.

Evaluation fairness is insufficiently documented. Baselines appear to use results from heterogeneous backbones and resolutions, while RAD uses the recent DINOv3 at high resolution. The backbone study does not resolve this confound because competing methods are not rerun with the same frozen encoder, preprocessing, and compute budget.

Several empirical details weaken reliability: dataset-specific K and spatial radii are used without explaining the tuning protocol; uncertainty across few-shot reference selections is not reported; only one seed is used; and no validation protocol or statistical testing is provided.

Reproducibility remains incomplete because the fusion weights w_l are not specified, the abstract's code URL is blank, and runtime, peak memory, memory-bank size, retrieval implementation, and preprocessing/anomaly-map postprocessing details are not fully reported. These omissions are especially important because storage and latency are the method's principal tradeoffs.

Presentation contains some overstated or inaccurate conclusions, including calling the 3D-ADAM experiment a 3D evaluation despite using RGB only and asserting state of the art across all datasets even where image-level performance trails Dinomaly. The limitations section also understates dependence on alignment, frozen-encoder quality, and normal-memory coverage.

strengths: RAD is a simple, practically useful training-free detector: global reference selection, spatially constrained nearest-neighbor matching, and multi-layer feature fusion directly address plausible cross-category and cross-region mismatches.

The empirical study is unusually broad, covering MVTec-AD, VisA, Real-IAD, a preliminary RGB-only 3D-ADAM evaluation, few-shot regimes, data scaling, incremental class onboarding, encoder choice, resolution, efficiency, and unseen-normal behavior.

Reported localization performance is strong. For example, Table 1 reports sizable P-AP/P-F1 gains over Dinomaly on MVTec-AD and Real-IAD, while Appendix Table A6 retains P-AP gains of 2.7 on MVTec-AD and 6.0 on MVTec-AD2 with a shared DINOv3-B backbone.

The component ablation in Table A5 supports the value of multi-layer retrieval, global conditioning, and spatial conditioning. Table A7 provides useful sensitivity sweeps, and the coreset experiment reduces MVTec-AD memory from 32.6 GB to 0.37 GB with modest degradation.
Presentation is generally clear and polished. The method is precisely described, the main figure is informative, and extensive per-category and qualitative results are provided.

The paper addresses a significant deployment concern: incorporating new normal data or categories without retraining. This is particularly valuable for cold-start and continually changing industrial systems.
The authors candidly acknowledge memory and latency costs and quantify both rather than concealing them. No intrinsically problematic data collection or human-subject issues are apparent.
weaknesses: The claimed fidelity-stability dilemma is not established by the theory. Lemma 2.2 only lower-bounds the decoder Jacobian, not the Jacobian of the composite reconstruction map or the residual score. Contraction by the bottleneck can cancel decoder expansion. Indeed, Assumption 2.1 implies that R-I is locally eta-Lipschitz along benign directions, which supports residual stability rather than the manuscript's claim that residual scores inevitably amplify benign perturbations.

The assertion that an information-losing bottleneck inevitably creates nonzero normal reconstruction error is also too strong. A bottleneck can remain injective on the normal manifold or memorize a finite training set. The paper provides no empirical measurement connecting bottleneck singular values, decoder gain, reconstruction fidelity, and false positives, so the proposed dilemma remains largely speculative.

The retrieval guarantees do not apply to the implemented RAD score. The proofs concern distance to one fixed set under a norm, whereas RAD uses query-dependent top-K global retrieval, spatially dependent candidate sets, cosine dissimilarity, multi-layer fusion, and image pooling. Top-K set changes can be discontinuous, invalidating the stated non-expansiveness argument for the actual detector.

The maximality and near-optimality results are weak evidence of anomaly-detection quality: distance-to-set is maximal only within a deliberately restricted class of 1-Lipschitz scores that vanish on the memory, and zero score on stored samples is an interpolation property rather than generalization. The reported mean normal-patch distance of 0.024 is insufficient without scale, distribution, anomaly-distance, and correspondence to the actual conditioned multi-layer score.

Originality is modest. The method principally combines established ingredients from PatchCore/SPADE-style frozen-feature nearest-neighbor detection—multi-layer features, global retrieval, and positional neighborhoods—with a newer DINOv3 backbone. The paper does not sharply distinguish these components from prior position-aware and unified memory-based detectors beyond empirical ablations.

Comparison fairness remains uncertain because most baselines in Table 1 use different backbones and possibly different input resolutions. The same-backbone comparison is limited to Dinomaly and two MVTec datasets; it does not cover VisA or Real-IAD. Thus, the broad claim that retrieval surpasses trained MUAD methods is not cleanly separated from the advantage of DINOv3 and 448x448 inputs.

There are unexplained numerical inconsistencies. For MVTec-AD, Table 1 and Tables 3/A2 report P-AUPRO 94.9, while the mean in per-category Table A11 is 95.8; image-level means also differ between Table 1 and Table A10. If these use micro versus macro aggregation, the protocol must be stated and applied consistently to baselines.

The evaluation reports only one seed and no uncertainty. Few-shot reference sampling, fraction scaling, and incremental-class subset selection can have substantial variance, yet confidence intervals or repeated subsets are absent. The criteria for selecting the fixed and target classes are also not specified, leaving room for favorable choices.

Dataset-specific K and spatial radii are used, including K=900 and different radii for every benchmark, but the paper does not explain how these were selected without anomaly-test labels. Sensitivity analysis is only on MVTec-AD. This is a reproducibility and possible test-set-tuning concern.

Reproducibility details remain incomplete: the exact DINOv3 checkpoint and normalization, interpolation and anomaly-map postprocessing, memory datatype, nearest-neighbor implementation, coreset algorithm/budget selection, subset sampling procedure, and baseline retraining protocols are not fully specified. The manuscript says code is available but displays no usable link.

The 3D-ADAM evidence is preliminary rather than support for a broad 3D claim: only RGB is used and comparison is limited to PatchCore and Dinomaly. Memory remains very large—up to 60.8 GB—and the compressed variant is tested only on MVTec-AD.

The limitations section honestly covers storage and latency, but omits important failure modes: sensitivity to spatial misalignment and global-retrieval errors, contamination of the normal memory, dependence on foundation-model pretraining, and operational consequences of false negatives. The impact statement's claim that no societal consequences need highlighting is too cursory for industrial inspection settings. Overall, the strong empirical promise is outweighed by unsupported central theoretical claims and evaluation/reproducibility ambiguities that require substantial revision.

strengths: The empirical results are broad and strong: RAD is evaluated on MVTec-AD, VisA, Real-IAD, and 3D-ADAM, with especially substantial gains in pixel-level AP and F1. The same-backbone comparison against Dinomaly on MVTec-AD and MVTec-AD2 helps show that the gains are not solely due to DINOv3.

The method is simple and practically useful. Global reference retrieval, spatially constrained patch matching, and multi-layer feature fusion are clearly described, and the ablation in Table A5 indicates that each component contributes.

The paper examines several relevant deployment regimes, including few-shot learning, progressive class onboarding, latency, memory usage, coreset compression, backbone choice, input resolution, and unseen-normal samples.
The manuscript is generally well organized and provides many implementation details, per-category results, qualitative examples, and an honest discussion of storage and inference costs.
weaknesses: The central fidelity-stability theory does not establish the claimed dilemma. Lemma 2.2 only lower-bounds the norm of the decoder Jacobian. A large decoder Jacobian does not imply that the composite reconstruction map, or the residual score ||z-R(z)||, is unstable: the bottleneck can contract directions that the decoder subsequently expands, yielding a near-identity composite and a stable residual. Indeed, Assumption 2.1 directly assumes that R is locally near-identity, which makes the derivative of R-I small along the specified benign directions. The manuscript's leap from decoder gain to inevitable score instability is therefore unsupported.

The retrieval theory analyzes a different score from the implemented RAD algorithm. The proofs concern Euclidean distance to a fixed memory set, whereas RAD uses cosine dissimilarity, test-dependent top-K global retrieval, spatially varying candidate sets, and weighted layer fusion. The selected memory can change discontinuously with the test image, and 1-cosine similarity is proportional to squared Euclidean distance for normalized features, not the distance function proved to be 1-Lipschitz. Consequently, the non-expansiveness and near-optimality results do not apply to RAD as implemented.

The theoretical optimality result is weak and partly built into the comparison class: F_gamma is defined to contain only nonnegative 1-Lipschitz scores that vanish on every memory point, making distance-to-set pointwise maximal almost by definition. This says little about anomaly detection quality, since maximizing all off-memory scores can also increase false positives on unseen normal samples. The reported mean normal-memory distance of 0.024 is not connected quantitatively to detection error or to the actual conditioned cosine score.

The claimed equivalence between the finite-neighborhood fidelity condition in Eq. 4 and the Jacobian bound in Eq. 5 is incorrect as stated. The former implies a derivative bound under differentiability, but a pointwise Jacobian bound alone does not imply the uniform finite-radius condition without additional regularity assumptions.

Originality is limited. RAD combines established nearest-neighbor feature memories with global retrieval, positional neighborhoods, and multi-layer aggregation. These are sensible engineering choices, but the paper does not sufficiently distinguish them conceptually from PatchCore, SPADE, PNI, UniVAD, and other retrieval-based anomaly detectors. The expansive claim that the work overturns an assumption about task-specific training is stronger than the methodological novelty supports.

Experimental reliability is weaker than the breadth suggests. Dataset-specific K and spatial radii are used without a documented validation protocol, and the sensitivity sweeps appear to be reported on the evaluation benchmark itself. Few-shot and subsampling results use only seed 1, with no repeated reference-set sampling, uncertainty estimates, or significance tests; this is particularly problematic for one- and two-shot claims. Comparisons also mix backbones and resolutions in the main tables, while controlled same-backbone evidence is restricted to Dinomaly on only two datasets.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Although architecture, resolutions, layers, K, radii, pooling, software versions, and hardware are listed, the abstract's code link is blank, and important procedural details such as memory construction/compression, exact preprocessing, dataset split handling, reference sampling, baseline reproduction, and hyperparameter selection are insufficient for an independent reproduction.

The limitations section mentions memory and latency but omits the method's dependence on spatial alignment, foundation-model pretraining, normal-memory coverage, potentially anomalous global retrieval queries, and benchmark-specific parameter selection. The impact statement's assertion that no societal consequences need highlighting is too cursory for an industrial detection method, where false negatives and false positives could affect safety, quality control, and automation decisions. strengths: The empirical evaluation is broad and unusually thorough: RAD is tested on MVTec-AD, VisA, Real-IAD, and 3D-ADAM, across standard, few-shot, and incremental-class settings, using seven image- and pixel-level metrics. The strongest gains are on localization, including P-AP improvements over Dinomaly of 6.3 points on MVTec-AD and 10.9 points on Real-IAD.

The method is simple and practically useful. Global [CLS]-based filtering, spatially constrained patch matching, and multi-layer fusion form a coherent training-free detector that can add new categories by updating its memory rather than retraining. The cold-start and incremental-class experiments demonstrate the significance of this capability.

The paper includes meaningful controls: component ablations, per-category results, hyperparameter sweeps, unseen-normal false-positive analysis, encoder and resolution studies, and a same-backbone comparison against Dinomaly. With DINOv3-B for both methods, RAD retains gains on MVTec-AD and MVTec-AD2, supporting a contribution beyond backbone strength.

Efficiency limitations are quantified rather than hidden. The paper reports latency and memory on four datasets and shows that coreset compression reduces MVTec-AD storage from 32.6 GB to 0.37 GB with only a small performance loss. The presentation is generally clear, and the extensive appendix makes the empirical claims easy to inspect.
weaknesses: The claimed fidelity-stability dilemma is not established by the theory presented. Lemma 2.2 only lower-bounds the decoder Jacobian under a contracting bottleneck; it does not show that the composite reconstruction map or the residual score is unstable. Indeed, Assumption 2.1 directly requires the composite map to be near-identity along benign directions. Large decoder gain can simply compensate for bottleneck contraction without amplifying the end-to-end residual. No experiment measures the proposed fidelity-stability trade-off, so the paper should substantially narrow this central theoretical claim.

The retrieval optimality result is mathematically valid but limited: distance-to-memory is maximal only within the deliberately restricted class of nonnegative 1-Lipschitz scores that vanish exactly on the stored samples. It offers no comparison with reconstruction scores outside that class, and the expected-separation bound can be loose because it depends only on unseen-normal coverage. Calling retrieval near-optimal or principled evidence that it is generally 'better' is therefore stronger than the result supports.

The most relevant empirical control is missing: a same-backbone, same-resolution implementation of a strong nearest-neighbor baseline such as PatchCore. The only same-backbone comparison is against the reconstruction-based Dinomaly, where the MVTec-AD advantage is modest on P-F1 and AUPRO. Because RAD largely combines established memory retrieval, spatial conditioning, and multi-layer features, this control is important for assessing both originality and the source of its gains.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite many implementation details. The promised code link is blank, the coreset construction is unspecified, and the paper does not explain how dataset-specific K and neighborhood radii were selected without anomaly-label or test-set feedback. Only one seed is reported, and sensitivity is evaluated only on MVTec-AD; uncertainty across few-shot reference sampling is not reported.

The title and repeated claim that the results overturn the need for task-specific training are too broad. The evidence concerns several industrial visual benchmarks using a powerful pretrained DINOv3 encoder, substantial memory, dataset-specific hyperparameters, and mostly aligned imagery. The spatial prior may be less suitable under large pose or layout changes, while performance outside industrial anomaly detection is untested. The limitations section should acknowledge this scope, possible foundation-model data overlap, and the safety consequences of false negatives in manufacturing deployment.
